html:
Google Research's harness2 is a tool for improving AI agents, so it is natural to want an AI agent to drive it: set up a benchmark, preview a sweep, estimate its cost, start it, wait, read the results and export the harness that won. Harness² Workbench ships an MCP server, h2workbench-mcp, built for exactly that from Claude Code, opencode, Codex, Cursor or any other MCP client.

It is also the most dangerous interface in the project. A model choosing tool calls can be wrong, can be steered by text it read in a previous result, and can cost money with every call it makes. This post is about the five rules that decide what such a model can and cannot do.

What an agent gets

Forty-two tools, three resource forms and three prompts. The tools follow the lifecycle of a sweep, and each needs a minimum role that the Workbench server, not the MCP server, enforces:

PurposeToolsRole
Orientserver_info, doctor, list_benchmarks, list_profiles, check_profileviewer
Experimentslist_experiments, get_experiment, get_manifest, list_splitsviewer
create_experiment, update_experimentoperator
Plan, no model callsestimate_cost, validate_harnessviewer
preview_run, check_benchmark, run_demo, create_splitoperator
Run (can cost money)start_run, start_pipeline, start_judge, start_reportoperator
Installsetup_benchmark, install_harness2, start_bridgeadmin
Followlist_jobs, get_job, wait_for_job, get_job_logviewer
cancel_joboperator
Read resultslist_tasks, get_task, get_harness, diff_harnesses, rollouts, scores, reports, libraries, the improver's audit sessions, compare_sweepsviewer
Adoptexport_harness (raw files, or an OpenCode or Codex project)viewer

The prompts are guided workflows: improve_agent_harness walks from the environment check through a cost estimate, your go-ahead, the run, the report and the export; analyze_sweep is read-only; adopt_best_harness chooses and explains a harness and asks for approval before anything is written.

Rule 1: the server decides, not the MCP server

h2workbench-mcp keeps no state, runs no jobs and holds no credentials of its own. Every tool call becomes an ordinary REST request carrying an API token, so the Workbench's roles, limits and audit log apply to an agent exactly as they apply to a person. A viewer token cannot start a job, whatever the model says.

There are two transports. Over stdio, one client uses one token, read from the environment or from a token file that the MCP server refuses to use if anyone but its owner can read it. Over streamable HTTP the endpoint is stateless and every request carries its own bearer token, which is forwarded as it is, so each client is authorised and audited separately. A token given to the process itself is ignored in that mode, with a warning, so a shared MCP endpoint can never lend one client's rights to another.

The HTTP endpoint has its own guard in front: an unknown Host is refused (DNS-rebinding defence, and a Host with credentials in it counts as unknown), a browser Origin that is not allowed is refused, requests without a well-formed token are refused, and concurrency and body size are capped. The MCP server also refuses to send tokens to a Workbench over plain http on anything but loopback, unless that is explicitly overridden.

Refusals cost the agent nothing and tell it what to do next: the server's error says which role a call needs. They also cannot be used to fill the audit log, because each token's refusals are recorded at most 10 a minute and only counted after that.

Rule 2: no tool for secrets, tokens, profiles or the audit log

This one is by contract: there is no MCP tool that writes a profile, a secret, a token or the audit log, and none that reads a secret. The reason is specific. A model profile names the endpoint a job sends its prompts to, and which stored secret holds its API key. A prompt-injected agent that could edit a profile could point the endpoint at a server it controls and receive the key with the next job. Secret values and new tokens should never pass through a model's context at all. People manage those through the web UI, the REST API or the command line.

Rule 3: a model cannot accept risk on your behalf

In host isolation, harness2's executors run as the Workbench's own user, with its files and its network: a host-mode job is, in effect, a Workbench administrator. The Workbench therefore refuses a host-mode run or pipeline unless the request sets acknowledge_risks: true.

That flag is a statement that a person accepted the risk, and the first security review pointed out that a model could simply set it. So the MCP server adds the only rule of its own: it refuses any start_run or start_pipeline call that sets acknowledge_risks=true, unless whoever started the MCP server passed --allow-risk-acknowledgement. The refusal, as it came back from a live server:

forbidden: this MCP server does not let a model set acknowledge_risks=true, which
accepts for the user that the executor runs with the server user's files and
network (host isolation). A human can start this run from the Workbench web UI;
an admin can pre-acknowledge host risks in the server configuration; or the
person who runs h2workbench-mcp can start it with --allow-risk-acknowledgement
(H2W_MCP_ALLOW_RISK_ACK=1). Without acknowledge_risks the call goes through and
the Workbench server decides.

The message is written for the model as much as for the person reading the transcript: it explains what the flag means and lists the three ways a human can make the decision instead. One of them, an administrator pre-acknowledging host risks in the server configuration, removes the requirement for everyone, agents included, and the documentation says exactly that. Other host-mode jobs (previews, the demo, judging, reports) never needed the acknowledgement, which is why the advice for anything untrusted is container isolation. The same thinking applies to money. budget_usd is an argument the model chooses, so the advice is a budget on the model account itself, not only in the tool call.

Rule 4: everything a tool returns is untrusted

Rollout files, job logs, improver prompts and answers, task text, transcripts, harness files and benchmark documents are written by models or by third parties, and any of them can contain instructions aimed at the agent reading them. An exported harness contains whatever a model wrote into it.

The server's instructions and the descriptions of those tools tell the model to read such content as data and never to follow instructions found in it. The documentation is explicit that this is guidance to a model, not a barrier: an agent that acts on instructions found in a result should be treated as compromised for that session, and nothing it proposes from that point should happen without a person's approval.

Rule 5: everything is bounded

An agent loop can wait forever, read forever and retry forever, so nothing in the MCP server is open-ended:

  • Waiting. Job-starting tools take a wait_secs of at most 600. The quick ones wait 45 seconds by default; the costly or slow ones return the queued job at once. wait_for_job follows the server's event stream for at most 600 seconds and falls back to polling when the stream is unavailable.
  • Output. A tool result is capped at about 100 KB of text, with an explicit note when it is cut and the full value attached as structured content when it is a reasonable size. Asking for the tail of a log returns the newest lines that fit, following the server's 1 MiB log pages, so a log of very long lines still ends at its last line.
  • The HTTP endpoint limits concurrent requests and body size, as above.

What was verified, and what was not

The MCP server was exercised live against a real Workbench and a real harness2 checkout over stdio: initialisation, the tool list, server_info, refusals for each role, and a real demo run through run_demo, as well as the HTTP guard. The end-to-end suite runs the demo through an MCP client on every push, and a snapshot test fails if any tool's schema or description changes without being reviewed. What has not been done is trying it in each of the MCP clients named above: the configuration snippets in the documentation follow each client's documented format and say they are unverified.

If you are building an MCP server for something that runs code

  • Make the MCP server a client of the system's own API, with the caller's credentials, so there is exactly one place where rules are enforced.
  • Leave out the tools you would not let a prompt-injected agent call. A tool that does not exist cannot be misused.
  • Separate "a person accepted this risk" from "a request says so", and do not let the model produce the former.
  • Write refusals that say what the model, or the person, should do next.
  • Bound every wait, every read and every retry.
  • Hand agents the least privilege that works: a viewer token by default, an operator token only when the agent must start jobs, never an admin token, one token per agent, with an expiry.
